content.what_the_parallel_cli_is_and_where_it_fi:
Parallel CLI is a terminal interface to Parallel's web-intelligence stack. The current documentation describes it as supporting web search, content extraction, data enrichment, deep research, entity discovery, and web monitoring. This is broader than the initial launch announcement, which highlighted search, extract, research, and enrich; for current command coverage, the documentation is the better source. [what_the_parallel_cli_is_and_where_it_fits[0]] [2] [what_the_parallel_cli_is_and_where_it_fits[1]] [1]

A minimal installation is:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://parallel.ai/install.sh | bash
export PARALLEL_API_KEY="your_api_key"
```

The documented package alternatives include `pipx install "parallel-web-tools[cli]"`, `uv tool install "parallel-web-tools[cli]"`, Homebrew, and npm. Interactive authentication uses `parallel-cli login`; SSH, containers, CI, and other headless environments can use `parallel-cli login --device`; `parallel-cli auth` checks the authentication state. [what_the_parallel_cli_is_and_where_it_fits[0]] [2]

The current command tree is useful because it exposes both short-lived and asynchronous operations:

```text
parallel-cli search
parallel-cli extract
parallel-cli research run|status|poll|processors
parallel-cli enrich suggest|plan|run|status|poll
parallel-cli findall run|entity-search|status|poll|result|cancel
parallel-cli monitor create|list|get|update|cancel|events|trigger
```

All documented commands support `--json`, which is the appropriate mode for an agent that must parse results rather than read terminal prose. Research, enrichment, and FindAll support `--no-wait`, followed by status or polling commands; Monitor has its own lifecycle commands for events and triggering a run. [what_the_parallel_cli_is_and_where_it_fits[0]] [2]

The design implication is that the CLI is not merely a human convenience. It is a stable process boundary: an agent can write JSON to a file, pass an identifier to a later polling step, and retain the raw result alongside its final answer. For applications that need high-throughput orchestration, webhooks, custom retries, or direct control over API fields, use the corresponding API while keeping the CLI as a debugging and local-agent interface. This division is a recommendation based on the documented command and lifecycle surfaces.
content.search_and_extract_a_two_stage_evidence_:
Search is the fast discovery layer. Its API accepts a natural-language objective and optional search queries, and returns relevant pages with LLM-optimized excerpts. The documented response can include a search ID, result URLs, titles, publication dates, excerpts, warnings, usage, and a session ID. The CLI exposes date filters, domain inclusion and exclusion, result limits, and search modes including `turbo`, `basic`, and `advanced`. [search_and_extract_a_two_stage_evidence_pipeline[0]] [35] [search_and_extract_a_two_stage_evidence_pipeline[1]] [38]

Useful agent commands include:

```sh
parallel-cli search "What is Anthropic's latest AI model?" --json
parallel-cli search -q "bitcoin price" --after-date 2026-01-01 --json
parallel-cli search "SEC filings for Apple" --include-domains sec.gov --json
parallel-cli search "latest AI research" --mode turbo --json
```

The mechanism is query expansion and ranking rather than page-by-page browsing. A research agent can use Search to identify likely primary sources, select the URLs that satisfy its source policy, and then call Extract only on those URLs. Turbo is documented as the lower-latency mode, while the default advanced mode is oriented toward higher quality; choose based on whether the next step is a quick routing decision or an evidence-sensitive answer. [search_and_extract_a_two_stage_evidence_pipeline[0]] [35] [search_and_extract_a_two_stage_evidence_pipeline[2]] [46]

Extract is the evidence-reading layer. It converts public URLs into clean, LLM-optimized Markdown, including JavaScript-heavy pages and PDFs, and can return objective-focused excerpts or full content. The CLI examples are:

```sh
parallel-cli extract https://example.com --json
parallel-cli extract https://company.com \
  --objective "Find pricing tiers, annual costs, and contract terms" --json
parallel-cli extract https://example.com --full-content --json
```

The Extract response includes result URLs, titles, publication dates, excerpts, and optionally full content, as well as top-level errors, warnings, usage, and session information. A practical use case is a filing or investor document: Search finds the relevant filing, and Extract focuses the long page on revenue, risk factors, or a specified clause. Parallel specifically describes Extract as useful for long or dense sources such as a 200-page SEC filing or investor document. [search_and_extract_a_two_stage_evidence_pipeline[3]] [36] [search_and_extract_a_two_stage_evidence_pipeline[4]] [7]

There are two important controls. Extract is a public-URL workflow, so access-controlled material is not the same as a successful extraction. Also, Search publication dates may be null and excerpts may be incomplete or truncated. Preserve the source URL, returned warnings, and extracted evidence rather than treating a clean Markdown response as proof that the source was complete. [search_and_extract_a_two_stage_evidence_pipeline[0]] [35] [search_and_extract_a_two_stage_evidence_pipeline[3]] [36]
content.deep_research_when_a_task_run_beats_a_sh:
The Task API and its CLI path, `parallel-cli research run`, are designed for open-ended questions where the agent does not begin with a structured set of rows to enrich. The workflow performs multi-source searching, reading, cross-referencing, and report generation. This is a different mechanism from Search, which returns retrieval results, and from Extract, which reads URLs supplied by the caller. [deep_research_when_a_task_run_beats_a_shell_loop[0]] [13] [deep_research_when_a_task_run_beats_a_shell_loop[1]] [1]

A practical command is:

```sh
parallel-cli research run \
  "Compare North American uranium supply chains, key companies, policy risks, and 2026 capacity constraints" \
  --processor ultra --no-wait --json
```

The command returns a run identifier rather than forcing an agent to block. The documented follow-up pattern is:

```sh
parallel-cli research status trun_xxx --json
parallel-cli research poll trun_xxx --json
parallel-cli research processors --json
```

The CLI documentation describes processor choices ranging from faster lookups to deeper multi-source synthesis; it also notes that the Ultra range may take up to 25 minutes. Pricing is processor-dependent and is charged per 1,000 Task runs, so the right design is to route simple questions to Search or Extract and reserve high-compute processors for questions that genuinely require breadth, reconciliation, and a narrative report. [deep_research_when_a_task_run_beats_a_shell_loop[2]] [2] [deep_research_when_a_task_run_beats_a_shell_loop[3]] [16]

The output is useful to an agent because it carries more than a paragraph of prose. The documented Task and CLI materials describe citations, reasoning or basis information, and calibrated confidence signals. An agent can therefore apply a policy such as: accept a high-confidence answer only if it has multiple relevant citations; otherwise ask for another run, narrow the question, or escalate to a human. The policy is a recommended control, while the presence of citations and confidence information is documented. [deep_research_when_a_task_run_beats_a_shell_loop[0]] [13] [deep_research_when_a_task_run_beats_a_shell_loop[2]] [2]

Good deep-research use cases include supply-chain mapping, competitive landscape reports, vendor due diligence, policy comparisons, and market or technology reviews. Poor use cases include a single known fact, a single known URL, or a repeated CRM field lookup. In those cases the shell loop is more observable and usually cheaper: Search identifies evidence, Extract reads it, and the agent writes a small structured result.
content.findall_and_enrich_turning_natural_langu:
FindAll is the discovery-to-dataset path. Its input is a natural-language objective such as finding AI companies that raised a particular funding round or residential roofing companies in a specified city. The system converts the objective into a schema with an entity type and match conditions, then creates a run, evaluates candidates, and returns a structured result. Supported entity categories include companies, people, products, and other real-world entities. [findall_and_enrich_turning_natural_language_into_structured_datasets[0]] [14]

The documented lifecycle is:

1. Convert the natural-language objective into a schema.
2. Review or modify the schema and create an asynchronous run.
3. Poll the run until it reaches a terminal state.
4. Retrieve the result snapshot.

The current CLI exposes the same pattern:

```sh
parallel-cli findall run "AI startups in healthcare" --json
parallel-cli findall run "Find roofing companies in Charlotte NC" -g base -n 25 --json
parallel-cli findall status findall_xxx --json
parallel-cli findall poll findall_xxx --json
parallel-cli findall result findall_xxx --json
```

It also exposes a faster entity-search path for a bounded lookup:

```sh
parallel-cli findall entity-search \
  "AI startups in San Francisco" \
  --entity-type companies --match-limit 25 --json
```

FindAll first generates candidates and then evaluates each candidate against every match condition. Results can include a candidate ID, name, URL, description, match status, output fields, run metrics, and a basis containing reasoning, confidence, citations, and source excerpts. Because snapshots may include candidates with `generated`, `matched`, or `unmatched` states, downstream code should filter on `match_status` instead of assuming every returned row passed every condition. [findall_and_enrich_turning_natural_language_into_structured_datasets[0]] [14]

Enrichment is deliberately separate from matching. A field that determines whether an entity belongs in the dataset is a match condition; an additional field such as employee count, technology stack, headquarters, revenue, or a recent event is enrichment and should not silently change the match decision. The FindAll documentation says enrichment data is extracted for matched candidates, using the Task API, and does not affect match conditions. [findall_and_enrich_turning_natural_language_into_structured_datasets[1]] [44] [findall_and_enrich_turning_natural_language_into_structured_datasets[2]] [25]

The standalone CLI `enrich` is the batch-context path. It accepts inline JSON or CSV/JSON sources, lets the caller describe source columns, takes a natural-language intent, and writes an enriched target:

```sh
parallel-cli enrich run \
  --source-type csv --source companies.csv --target enriched.csv \
  --source-columns '[{"name":"company","description":"Company name"}]' \
  --intent "Find the CEO, headquarters, and annual revenue"
```

The CLI launch material describes enrichment as priced per row rather than per output field, and describes a range from small lookups on lighter processors to 20 or more fields on the deepest processor. Treat those statements as product documentation, then confirm current pricing and processor availability before budgeting a production job. [findall_and_enrich_turning_natural_language_into_structured_datasets[3]] [1] [findall_and_enrich_turning_natural_language_into_structured_datasets[4]] [16]

The practical distinction is simple: FindAll creates the rows; Enrich adds web context to rows that already exist. Together they support lead generation, account intelligence, research databases, talent or company discovery, and recurring data refreshes. Entity resolution remains a design responsibility: pass stable identifiers or domains when available, inspect citations, and do not write ambiguous matches directly into a CRM.
content.monitor_converting_web_change_into_agent:
Monitor is the continuous layer. A monitor stores a natural-language query in its settings, runs it on a schedule, and surfaces new relevant information. The current CLI exposes creation, listing, retrieval, update, cancellation, event retrieval, and manual triggering. [monitor_converting_web_change_into_agent_events[0]] [21] [monitor_converting_web_change_into_agent_events[1]] [2]

Examples:

```sh
parallel-cli monitor create "New AI funding announcements" \
  --frequency 1h --json

parallel-cli monitor create "SEC filings from Tesla" \
  --webhook https://example.com/hook --json

parallel-cli monitor list --json
parallel-cli monitor events mon_xxx --json
parallel-cli monitor trigger mon_xxx --json
parallel-cli monitor update mon_xxx --frequency 1w --json
```

There are two distinct monitoring mechanisms. An `event_stream` monitor reports newly detected changes, which is appropriate for news, funding, filings, product announcements, and competitor events. A snapshot monitor tracks an evolving structured result, such as the output of a Task run, and reports material changes to that result. The CLI documents snapshot creation with `--type snapshot --task-run-id trun_xxx`. [monitor_converting_web_change_into_agent_events[0]] [21] [monitor_converting_web_change_into_agent_events[2]] [22]

The documented frequency examples include `1h`, `1d`, and `1w`; the monitor runs once immediately when created and then follows its schedule. Webhooks can subscribe to monitor event types such as `monitor.event.detected`. Event retrieval includes an event ID, event group ID, event date, event type, and output. The output can carry typed content plus basis information such as citations, reasoning, and confidence. [monitor_converting_web_change_into_agent_events[0]] [21] [monitor_converting_web_change_into_agent_events[3]] [20]

Monitor also filters duplicates based on what it has surfaced in previous runs. That is valuable for alert fatigue, but it changes the meaning of the feed: it is a stream of relevant new events, not an archive of every repeated page observation. Use event groups and stored evidence to make downstream processing idempotent; use snapshots when the business question is whether a structured state changed. [monitor_converting_web_change_into_agent_events[4]] [23] [monitor_converting_web_change_into_agent_events[3]] [20]

A production pattern is: Monitor receives a new filing or funding event, a webhook invokes an agent, Extract reads the primary source, and the agent updates a CRM, risk register, or internal digest. The recommendation follows from the documented webhook, event, and Extract surfaces; teams should still impose source allowlists and human approval before taking an external action.
content.real_world_cases_opendoor_finch_genpact_:
### Opendoor: HOA verification

Opendoor's case study describes an HOA research workflow in its AI-native real-estate operations. The reported change is concrete: a manual process that took 10 minutes became a two-minute verification step when Parallel served as the web-research layer. [real_world_cases_opendoor_finch_genpact_and_actively[0]] [34]

The lesson is not simply that web research can be faster. The workflow has a bounded input, a repeatable question about a property, and a verification output that can be inserted into an operating process. That makes Search and Extract, or a focused Task run, more appropriate than an unconstrained research report. The time comparison is a customer case-study claim, so it should be validated against a team's own sample before becoming an SLA.

### Finch: case-relevant legal facts

Finch's case study describes AI agents running structured research workflows for plaintiff law, pulling case-relevant facts from the public web, enriching records, and feeding the results into downstream work. [real_world_cases_opendoor_finch_genpact_and_actively[1]] [33]

This illustrates the FindAll and Enrich pattern even when the full product surface is not exposed in the case description: define the record, gather web evidence, add structured fields, and pass the result to a domain workflow. Legal use also exposes the risk boundary. Case relevance and citation quality matter more than a fluent summary, so the basis, source URLs, and human review should be retained for any consequential filing or claim decision.

### Genpact: insurance and sales research

Genpact's partnership announcement says integrating Parallel's API helps automate and improve research workflows in insurance and sales. The use case is valuable because it spans two different kinds of work: structured operational research in insurance and prospect or client research for commercial teams. [real_world_cases_opendoor_finch_genpact_and_actively[2]] [32]

The mechanism is reusable: an agent retrieves current public information, converts it into structured evidence, and places the result where an analyst or seller can act. The announcement establishes the workflow direction, but it does not by itself establish a universal accuracy or return-on-investment number. Treat the case as evidence that these workflows are being attempted in production, not as proof that every insurer or sales organization will see the same outcome.

### Actively: account intelligence and buying signals

Actively's case study presents Per Account Agents that continuously reason across the web, surface buying signals, and move accounts through a revenue workflow. It reports that customers using Actively with Parallel's web-intelligence APIs see 23% higher win rates. [real_world_cases_opendoor_finch_genpact_and_actively[3]] [39]

This is the Monitor-plus-Task pattern: continuous signal collection supplies context, and a research agent interprets that context for an account. The metric is reported by the case study and should be treated as a customer or vendor-reported claim until independently reproduced. The strategic takeaway is stronger than the number: agents create value when web retrieval is connected to a decision process, not when it merely produces another standalone answer.
content.implementation_playbook_and_failure_cont:
A compact end-to-end shell workflow can look like this:

```sh
export PARALLEL_API_KEY="your_api_key"

# 1. Discover candidate sources
parallel-cli search "Latest SEC filings and earnings risks for Company X" \
  --include-domains sec.gov --mode advanced --json > search.json

# 2. Read a selected source with a focused objective
parallel-cli extract "https://example.com/filing" \
  --objective "Extract revenue guidance, risk factors, and cited dates" \
  --json > evidence.json

# 3. Start an open-ended investigation when synthesis is required
parallel-cli research run "Assess Company X supply-chain exposure" \
  --processor base --no-wait --json > task.json
parallel-cli research poll trun_xxx --json > report.json

# 4. Build or enrich structured records
parallel-cli findall run "AI infrastructure companies in Europe" \
  -g base -n 100 --no-wait --json > entities.json
parallel-cli enrich run --source-type csv --source companies.csv \
  --target enriched.csv \
  --source-columns '[{"name":"company","description":"Legal or brand name"}]' \
  --intent "Find headquarters, founders, and latest funding" \
  --json

# 5. Watch for changes
parallel-cli monitor create "New funding or acquisition news for Company X" \
  --frequency 1d --json > monitor.json
```

The exact identifiers and output files should be treated as state. Store the search ID, task or FindAll run ID, monitor ID, source URL, publication date when present, warnings, and basis or citation fields. For FindAll, reject or quarantine rows whose `match_status` is not `matched`; for Search and Extract, surface missing publication dates and extraction errors instead of silently substituting a current-looking page. These controls follow the documented output and status fields. [implementation_playbook_and_failure_controls[0]] [2] [implementation_playbook_and_failure_controls[1]] [14] [implementation_playbook_and_failure_controls[2]] [35] [implementation_playbook_and_failure_controls[3]] [36]

Use separate acceptance tests for each operation. Search should be measured on relevant-source recall and citation quality. Extract should be measured on field completeness and whether the requested passages are present. FindAll should be measured on match precision, recall, duplicate rate, and entity-resolution accuracy. Task should be measured on factuality, citation coverage, latency, and cost. Monitor should be measured on time to detection, duplicate suppression, and missed material changes. These are implementation recommendations, not guarantees made by Parallel.

Finally, treat benchmark and case-study claims as directional evidence. Parallel's own search benchmark announcement reports up to 50% lower cost than some LLM-native web-search implementations, but a vendor benchmark is not an independent guarantee for a particular workload. Re-run a representative test set, compare against the incumbent, and set a budget cap before enabling high-volume Task, FindAll, or Monitor jobs. content.synthesis:
| Operation | Core mechanism | Best input | Typical output and lifecycle | Best fit | Main trade-off |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Search | Ranked web retrieval with focused excerpts | Natural-language objective and optional queries | Results with URLs, titles, dates, excerpts, warnings, and usage | Fast current answers and source discovery | Excerpts can be incomplete; it does not by itself produce a validated dataset or report. [synthesis[0]] [35] |
| Extract | Page or PDF conversion into focused Markdown | One or more public URLs plus an objective | Excerpts or full content, with errors and warnings | Reading a known source or selected search result | Depends on public URL accessibility and extraction completeness. [synthesis[1]] [36] |
| Task / Research | Multi-source search, reading, cross-checking, and synthesis | Open-ended research question | Asynchronous report with citations, basis or confidence information | Due diligence, landscape research, and complex comparisons | Higher latency and processor-dependent cost. [synthesis[2]] [13] |
| FindAll | Candidate generation followed by condition evaluation | Natural-language entity criteria | Asynchronous structured entity snapshot with match status and evidence | Building a company, people, product, or property universe | Candidate coverage and entity resolution require validation. [synthesis[3]] [14] |
| Enrich | Web research applied to existing rows | CSV, JSON, or inline records plus field intent | Enriched target records, optionally asynchronous | CRM, account, lead, and research-record enrichment | Cost and quality scale with row count; ambiguous identities can contaminate data. [synthesis[4]] [2] |
| Monitor | Scheduled query or snapshot change detection | Natural-language signal, schedule, and optional webhook | Deduplicated events or structured snapshots | News, filings, funding, prices, and changing Task outputs | Deduplication means the feed is not every repeated observation. [synthesis[5]] [23] [synthesis[6]] [20] |

The key contrast is scope. Search and Extract are synchronous evidence primitives; Task is a synthesis primitive; FindAll and Enrich are dataset primitives; Monitor is a temporal primitive. The second contrast is time horizon: Search and Extract answer now, Task answers after an asynchronous investigation, FindAll creates a point-in-time dataset, and Monitor maintains a signal over time. The third contrast is failure mode: retrieval can miss or truncate evidence, synthesis can overgeneralize, discovery can misresolve entities, and monitoring can suppress duplicates or miss a material change if the query is poorly specified.

For most agents, the recommended architecture is `Search -> Extract -> decision`. Add `Task` when the question is open-ended, `FindAll -> Enrich` when the output is a dataset, and `Monitor -> Extract -> Task` when new events need interpretation. Use the CLI for local development, terminal agents, and inspectable batch jobs; use the APIs directly when webhook delivery, scheduling, high concurrency, or custom lifecycle control is central. This architecture aligns the mechanism to the decision instead of treating every web question as a deep-research job.
